title: Building Block Adventures - Our First Steps with Blockly
subject: ICT
chapter: 34. Building Block Adventures - Our First Steps with Blockly
description: Explore Blockly programming basics: sequences, algorithms, decomposition, India's ancient algorithmic heritage (Panini, Brahmagupta, Al-Khwarizmi), repeat loops, repeat-until loops, nested loops, if and if-else statements, and the AND/OR logical operators.

questions.question: What is Blockly?
questions.explanation: Blockly lets you create programs using colourful blocks that snap together like puzzle pieces, instead of typing complicated code.
options: A programming tool that uses colourful blocks that snap together like puzzle pieces

questions.question: In Blockly, what do we call instructions carried out one after another, from first to last?
questions.explanation: A sequence is a set of instructions carried out one after another, in a specific order.

questions.question: True or False: Sequential programming means the computer reads instructions from top to bottom, one after another.
questions.explanation: This is exactly how the chapter defines sequential programming, and it is confirmed again in the Milestone B review.

questions.question: What is an algorithm, according to the chapter's very first activity (the garden maze)?
questions.explanation: The chapter defines an algorithm as a set of step-by-step instructions to solve a problem, illustrated by following arrows through a maze from start to finish.
options: A set of step-by-step instructions to solve a problem

questions.question: In the maze activity on the first page, what does each arrow represent?
questions.explanation: Each arrow works like a block of code that tells the character which direction to move.
options: A block of code that tells the character which direction to move

questions.question: How many total blocks (move forward + turn right combined) are used in the 'perfect square' example?
questions.explanation: The square example lists 7 numbered steps in total: 4 'move forward 100' blocks alternated with 3 'turn right 90 degrees' blocks.

questions.question: In the square-drawing example, how many times does the character turn right 90 degrees?
questions.explanation: The 7 steps alternate move, turn, move, turn, move, turn, move - so there are exactly 3 turn-right actions.

questions.question: In the square example, how many 'move forward by 100' blocks are used in total?
questions.explanation: The 7 steps include moves at positions 1, 3, 5, and 7 - four 'move forward by 100' blocks in total.

questions.question: If you changed the order of the blocks in a sequence in Blockly, what would most likely happen (per Checkpoint 1)?
questions.explanation: Checkpoint 1 asks this exact question - since a sequence runs blocks in order, changing that order changes the resulting path.
options: The Turtle will follow a different path
The program works exactly the same
The program will automatically fix itself
Blockly will delete the extra blocks

questions.question: According to Checkpoint 1, in what order does Blockly's computer execute instructions?
questions.explanation: Checkpoint 1 confirms that Blockly executes instructions in sequence from top to bottom.
options: In sequence from top to bottom
Only the brightly coloured blocks first

questions.question: Which of the following are true about sequences in Blockly? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Blocks snap together in order, run in that specific order, and are read top to bottom - the computer never picks blocks randomly.
options: Blocks connect together like puzzle pieces
Instructions run in a specific order
The computer decides randomly which block to run first
Sequential programs are read top to bottom

questions.question: True or False: In Blockly, you must type lines of code exactly like in a traditional programming language.
questions.explanation: Blockly avoids typing code - you drag and snap together colourful blocks instead.

questions.question: What was the very first activity in the chapter used to introduce the idea of an algorithm?
questions.explanation: The chapter opens with the garden maze 'Follow the Code Path' activity to introduce algorithms.
options: Following an arrow path through a garden maze
Drawing a perfect square with Blockly

questions.question: The chapter says a computer follows sequence instructions 'the exact order we give them' - similar to which two everyday examples given in the text?
questions.explanation: The chapter compares following steps in order to playing a musical instrument or following a treasure map.
options: Following steps to play a musical instrument, and following a treasure map
Watching TV and reading a book

questions.question: The Blockly Turtle 'Movement' category, mentioned in Cyber Station 1, is used for which purpose?
questions.explanation: Cyber Station 1 instructs students to find the 'Movement' category of blocks under 'Turtle' to move the character.
options: To drag and drop blocks that move the Turtle (like move forward, turn right, turn left)
To change the colour of the maze
To save your program to a file
To add sound effects to the program

questions.question: What is decomposition, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: Decomposition means breaking a big problem into smaller, manageable steps.
options: Breaking down a big problem into smaller, manageable steps
Adding more code to a program

questions.question: An algorithm is compared to which everyday example in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter describes an algorithm as a step-by-step set of instructions to solve a problem, like a recipe.

questions.question: True or False: Decomposition is one of the most important skills in programming.
questions.explanation: The chapter states decomposition is one of the most important skills in programming.

questions.question: In the maze decomposition example, what is the FIRST step listed?
questions.explanation: The 5-step maze decomposition example begins with 'Move forward'.

questions.question: In the maze decomposition example, what should the character do in step 3, if there IS a coin?
questions.explanation: Step 3 of the maze decomposition is 'If there is a coin, collect it'.

questions.question: In the maze decomposition example, what should the character do in step 5, if there IS an obstacle?
questions.explanation: Step 5 of the maze decomposition is 'If there is an obstacle, turn to avoid it'.

questions.question: The Trail Treasure box explains that the original 'turtle' (which inspired the Blockly Turtle) was:
questions.explanation: The Trail Treasure box explains the original turtle was a real wheeled robot built in the 1960s that drew on paper with a pen.
options: A real robot with wheels that drew on paper with a pen, built in the 1960s
A pet turtle owned by a computer scientist
A cartoon character from a video game

questions.question: Which everyday tasks are given as examples of algorithms we already use without thinking about it?
questions.explanation: The chapter gives tying shoes and brushing teeth as everyday examples of algorithms.
options: Watching a movie and eating popcorn
Painting a picture and singing a song
Riding in a car and looking out the window

questions.question: Which of these are steps in the 5-step maze decomposition example? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The 5 steps are: move forward, check for a coin, collect if present, check for an obstacle, turn to avoid it if present - deleting the maze is not one of them.
options: Check if there's an obstacle ahead

questions.question: Why is decomposition considered useful when programming a character to move through a maze?
questions.explanation: Decomposition breaks a complex task into small steps that are each easy to program.
options: Because it breaks a complex task (navigating and collecting coins) into small, manageable steps that are each easy to code
Because it makes the maze shorter
Because it deletes unnecessary blocks automatically
Because it changes the character's colour

questions.question: In the 'Getting Ready for School' activity, what skill are students practicing?
questions.explanation: The 'Getting Ready for School' activity is a decomposition exercise, breaking a task into steps.
options: Decomposition - breaking a task into steps

questions.question: The 'Getting Ready for School' activity asks students to reflect on which question?
questions.explanation: The reflection question asks which task needed more steps and why.
options: Which task needed more steps, and why
Which task took the least time

questions.question: In the Curiosity Cloud reflection about a robot setting the dinner table, which of these is listed as a simple instruction the robot might follow?
questions.explanation: The Curiosity Cloud lists simple instructions like pick up, move forward, turn left, and put down for the table-setting robot.

questions.question: True or False: According to the chapter, decomposition means solving a whole problem in a single giant step instead of breaking it into smaller ones.
questions.explanation: Decomposition is the opposite - breaking a big problem into smaller, manageable steps, not doing it in one giant step.

questions.question: Which of these decomposition steps for the maze character checks a condition (asks a question) rather than performing a direct action?
questions.explanation: 'Check if there's a coin' asks a yes/no question, while the others are direct actions.

questions.question: Who wrote the Ashtadhyayi, a Sanskrit grammar made of nearly 4,000 ordered rules called sutras?
questions.explanation: Panini wrote the Ashtadhyayi around 500 BCE.

questions.question: Around what time period did Panini write the Ashtadhyayi?
questions.explanation: The chapter states Panini wrote the Ashtadhyayi around 500 BCE.

questions.question: Why do computer scientists today consider Panini's Ashtadhyayi the world's first formal algorithmic system?
questions.explanation: The rules (sutras) were so precise that computer scientists today consider it the world's first formal algorithmic system.
options: Because its nearly 4,000 rules (sutras) were so precise and ordered
Because it was written using a computer
Because it was translated into English
Because it describes the Blockly Turtle

questions.question: Who wrote step-by-step methods for solving complex maths problems in the 7th century CE, over a thousand years before European mathematicians did the same?
questions.explanation: Brahmagupta wrote these step-by-step maths methods in the 7th century CE.

questions.question: According to the chapter, where does the word 'algorithm' come from?
questions.explanation: The word 'algorithm' comes from Al-Khwarizmi, a Persian scholar connected to India's decimal number system.
options: The Persian scholar Al-Khwarizmi, who studied and extended India's decimal number system
The name of a Blockly programmer

questions.question: What did Al-Khwarizmi study and extend, which we still use today as Hindu-Arabic numerals?
questions.explanation: Al-Khwarizmi studied and extended India's decimal number system, giving us the Hindu-Arabic numerals used today.

questions.question: True or False: The idea of an algorithm began only after computers were invented.
questions.explanation: India's scholars were writing algorithms (precise step-by-step methods) thousands of years before computers existed.

questions.question: What are the individual ordered rules in Panini's Ashtadhyayi called?
questions.explanation: Panini's Ashtadhyayi is made up of nearly 4,000 ordered rules called sutras.

questions.question: According to the chapter's reflection, what are you doing every time you write a Blockly sequence?
questions.explanation: The reflection states that writing a Blockly sequence is the same as what Panini did - giving precise, ordered instructions.
options: The same thing Panini did - giving precise, ordered instructions
Something completely different from ancient algorithms

questions.question: Which historical figures are mentioned in the 'Heritage Route: India's Ancient Algorithms' section? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Panini, Brahmagupta, and Al-Khwarizmi are all discussed; Isaac Newton is not mentioned.

questions.question: Approximately how many ordered rules (sutras) are in Panini's Ashtadhyayi?
questions.explanation: The chapter states the Ashtadhyayi has nearly 4,000 ordered rules (sutras).

questions.question: True or False: Brahmagupta's step-by-step maths methods came AFTER European mathematicians developed similar methods.
questions.explanation: Brahmagupta's methods (7th century CE) came over a thousand years BEFORE European mathematicians developed similar methods, per the chapter.

questions.question: Al-Khwarizmi is described in the chapter as a scholar from which region?
questions.explanation: The chapter identifies Al-Khwarizmi as a Persian scholar.

questions.question: What connects Panini's ancient work to modern Blockly programming, according to the chapter's reflection?
questions.explanation: The reflection connects Panini's precise, ordered sutras to the precise, ordered instructions of a Blockly sequence.
options: Both involve giving precise, ordered instructions

questions.question: What does the chapter mean by saying 'ancient wisdom and modern coding share the same DNA'?
questions.explanation: This phrase means the precise, step-by-step thinking of ancient scholars like Panini is the same kind of thinking used in coding today.
options: The step-by-step, precise thinking behind ancient Indian scholarship (like Panini's sutras) is the same kind of thinking used in writing a Blockly sequence today
Modern coding replaced ancient wisdom completely

questions.question: What is the simplest type of loop in Blockly, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter describes the repeat block as the simplest loop.

questions.question: Without loops, how many times would you need to repeat the same instructions to draw 100 stars?
questions.explanation: Without loops, drawing 100 stars would require writing the same instructions 100 times.

questions.question: To draw a square using a repeat loop, how many times should you repeat the block 'move forward 100, turn right 90 degrees'?
questions.explanation: A square is drawn using a repeat loop that runs 4 times.

questions.question: To draw a pentagon using a repeat loop, what turn angle should be used (instead of the square's 90 degrees)?
questions.explanation: A pentagon uses a turn angle of 72 degrees instead of the square's 90 degrees.

questions.question: To draw a pentagon instead of a square with a repeat loop, how many times should the loop repeat?
questions.explanation: A pentagon's repeat loop runs 5 times instead of the square's 4 times.

questions.question: What TWO things must you change to turn a 'draw a square' repeat-loop program into a 'draw a pentagon' program?
questions.explanation: You only need to change the repeat count from 4 to 5 and the turn angle from 90 to 72 degrees.
options: The number of repetitions (4 to 5) and the turn angle (90 degrees to 72 degrees)
The colour of the blocks and the size of the screen
The starting position and the Turtle's name

questions.question: True or False: A loop lets you repeat instructions multiple times without having to rewrite them each time.
questions.explanation: This is exactly how loops are described in the chapter.

questions.question: What is the goal of 'Cyber Station 2: Loop Magic'?
questions.explanation: Cyber Station 2's goal is to use repeat loops to create geometric shapes efficiently.
options: To use repeat loops to create geometric shapes efficiently
To draw a maze from scratch
To combine AND and OR operators

questions.question: In Cyber Station 2, which shape requires changing both the number of sides AND the turn angle compared to a square?
questions.explanation: Cyber Station 2 asks students to modify the square program to draw a triangle by changing the number of sides and the turn angle.

questions.question: According to Cyber Station 2, how would you make a shape closer to a circle using repeat loops?
questions.explanation: Cyber Station 2's challenge suggests using many repetitions with small turn angles to approximate a circle.
options: Use a very large number of repetitions with very small turns (many, many sides)

questions.question: According to the Trail Treasure box, at what age did Bill Gates write his first computer program?
questions.explanation: The Trail Treasure box states Bill Gates wrote his first computer program at age 13.

questions.question: Why is Blockly designed with colourful blocks and shapes, according to the Trail Treasure box on page 40?
questions.explanation: The Trail Treasure box explains Blockly is designed so even non-readers can code, using shape and colour cues.
options: So that even children who cannot read yet can still code
So that only adults can use it
So that it looks nice on posters
So that it works without a computer

questions.question: Which of these shapes are mentioned as ones you could draw using repeat loops in Cyber Station 2? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Cyber Station 2 mentions drawing a square, triangle, and hexagon using repeat loops.

questions.question: A hexagon has six sides. If you used a repeat loop to draw one, how many times would the loop need to repeat the 'move forward, turn' pair?
questions.explanation: Following the same pattern as the square (4 times) and pentagon (5 times), a six-sided hexagon needs the loop to repeat 6 times.

questions.question: What must you specify when using a 'repeat' block in Blockly?
questions.explanation: A repeat block requires you to specify how many times to repeat the instructions.
options: How many times to repeat the instructions
What colour the block should be

questions.question: True or False: The chapter states that loops make repetitive tasks easier by letting you repeat blocks instead of rewriting the same instructions many times.
questions.explanation: This matches the chapter's description of why loops are useful.

questions.question: When should you use a 'Repeat Until' block instead of a regular 'Repeat' block?
questions.explanation: Repeat Until is used when you don't know exactly how many times to repeat instructions.
options: When you don't know exactly how many times you need to repeat something
When you always know the exact number of repetitions
When you want the loop to never stop
When you want to skip the condition entirely

questions.question: What is a 'condition' in a Repeat Until block?
questions.explanation: A condition is a question answered yes/no (true/false).
options: A question that is answered yes or no (true or false)
A colour chosen for the block

questions.question: Which of these is given as an example of using a Repeat Until loop?
questions.explanation: 'Repeat until the character reaches a wall' is one of the chapter's Repeat Until examples.
options: Repeat until the character reaches a wall
Repeat exactly 4 times to draw a square
Repeat exactly 5 times to draw a pentagon

questions.question: Which of these are given as Repeat Until examples in the chapter? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The chapter gives three Repeat Until examples: reaching a wall, collecting all coins, and the timer reaching zero.
options: Repeat until the character reaches a wall
Repeat until all coins are collected
Repeat until the timer reaches zero

questions.question: What does a Repeat Until block do after each repetition?
questions.explanation: The Repeat Until block keeps checking the condition after each repetition.
options: It checks the condition again to see if it should stop
It changes into a Repeat block

questions.question: If the condition inside a Repeat Until block is met (answer is 'yes'), what happens?
questions.explanation: If the condition is met, the loop stops.
options: The loop starts over from the very beginning
The loop repeats one more time no matter what

questions.question: True or False: A Repeat block and a Repeat Until block work in exactly the same way.
questions.explanation: A 'Repeat N times' block always runs exactly N times, while a 'Repeat Until' block checks a condition after every run and only stops once that condition becomes true - it could run a different number of times each time.

questions.question: Why is it a myth that 'Repeat Until' and 'Repeat' are the same thing?
questions.explanation: The Detour myth-busting box explains this exact distinction between Repeat and Repeat Until.
options: Because 'Repeat' always runs a fixed number of times, while 'Repeat Until' keeps checking a condition and could run a different number of times each time the program runs
Because 'Repeat' cannot be used to draw shapes
Because 'Repeat Until' only works with the colour blue

questions.question: If you use 'Repeat Until the character reaches a wall', and the wall is very close, roughly how many times might the loop run compared to if the wall were very far away?
questions.explanation: Since Repeat Until depends on a condition (distance to the wall) rather than a fixed count, it runs fewer times when the wall is close.
options: Fewer times than if the wall were far away
Exactly the same number of times regardless of distance

questions.question: In Blockly, a condition (used in blocks like Repeat Until or If) is best described as:
questions.explanation: A condition is a question answered true or false.
options: A question that is answered true or false

questions.question: What kind of situation is a 'Repeat Until: all coins collected' loop useful for?
questions.explanation: Repeat Until is useful exactly when you don't know the number of repetitions in advance.
options: When you don't know in advance how many coins there are or how long it will take to collect them all
When you always collect exactly 5 coins
When there are no coins at all
When the Turtle should never stop moving

questions.question: True or False: A 'Repeat Until' loop could run 2 times in one situation and 200 times in another situation, depending on when its condition becomes true.
questions.explanation: The Detour myth-busting box explicitly states this variability of Repeat Until loops.

questions.question: What is checked EVERY time a Repeat Until loop finishes one repetition?
questions.explanation: After every repetition, the Repeat Until block checks whether its condition has become true.
options: Whether its condition has become true

questions.question: 'Repeat until the timer reaches zero' is an example of which type of Blockly loop?
questions.explanation: This is one of the chapter's three Repeat Until examples.

questions.question: Why can't we always know in advance exactly how many times a Repeat Until loop will run?
questions.explanation: Repeat Until depends on a condition becoming true, which can vary, so the exact number of repetitions can't always be known in advance.
options: Because it depends on when its condition becomes true, which can vary each time the program runs

questions.question: What is a nested loop?
questions.explanation: A nested loop is a loop placed inside another loop.
options: A loop placed inside another loop
A loop with no repeat count
A block used only for if-else logic

questions.question: What everyday comparison does the chapter use to describe nested loops?
questions.explanation: The chapter compares nested loops to wheels within wheels.

questions.question: To draw a 4x4 grid of stars with nested loops, how many times does the outer loop repeat?
questions.explanation: The outer loop repeats 4 times, once for each row.

questions.question: To draw a 4x4 grid of stars with nested loops, how many times does the inner loop repeat for EACH row?
questions.explanation: The inner loop repeats 4 times to draw each star in a single row.
options: 4 times (once per star in the row)

questions.question: If an outer loop repeats 4 times and an inner loop inside it repeats 4 times, how many total times do the inner loop's instructions run?
questions.explanation: The inner loop's instructions run once for every combination of outer and inner repetitions: 4 x 4 = 16 times.

questions.question: What word does the chapter use for 'doing something again and again'?
questions.explanation: The chapter uses the word 'iteration' for doing something again and again.

questions.question: In Skill Trail 2's Pattern 1 (outer loop repeats 3 times, inner loop repeats 4 times, drawing a star each time), how many total stars are drawn?
questions.explanation: 3 rows of 4 stars each = 12 stars total.

questions.question: In Skill Trail 2's Pattern 2 (outer loop repeats 4 times, inner loop repeats 5 times), how many total stars are drawn?
questions.explanation: 4 rows of 5 stars each = 20 stars total.

questions.question: Checkpoint 2 asks: a loop repeats 5 times, and inside it is another loop that repeats 3 times. What is the total number of actions?
questions.explanation: 5 x 3 = 15 total actions.

questions.question: According to Checkpoint 2, which type of loop is best for drawing a square (a shape with a fixed, known number of sides)?
questions.explanation: Since a square always needs exactly 4 sides (a known, fixed number), a simple repeat loop is best.

questions.question: True or False: In a nested loop, the OUTER loop's instructions run more often than the INNER loop's instructions.
questions.explanation: It is actually the opposite - the INNER loop runs most often. If an outer loop repeats 4 times and an inner loop repeats 3 times, the inner loop's instructions execute 4 x 3 = 12 times, while the outer loop's own instructions only run 4 times.

questions.question: If an outer loop repeats 4 times and an inner loop inside it repeats 3 times, how many times do the OUTER loop's OWN instructions (outside the inner loop) run?
questions.explanation: The outer loop's own instructions (outside the inner loop) run only 4 times, once per outer repetition.

questions.question: Nested loops are used to create:
questions.explanation: Nested loops create more complex patterns, like grids of stars.
options: More complex patterns, like grids of stars

questions.question: In the star-grid example, what does the outer loop control?
questions.explanation: The outer loop controls moving to a new row for each repetition.

questions.question: In the star-grid example, what does the inner loop control?
questions.explanation: The inner loop controls drawing each star within a single row.
options: Drawing each star within a single row

questions.question: Which of these are true about nested loops? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Nested loops are used to draw grids of stars, so the third option is false; the other three statements are all true.
options: A nested loop is a loop placed inside another loop
The inner loop completes fully each time the outer loop runs once
Nested loops can never be used to draw grids of stars
Iteration means doing something again and again

questions.question: What does an 'If' statement do in Blockly?
questions.explanation: An If statement checks a condition and only runs its blocks if that condition is true.
options: It checks a condition and runs certain blocks only if that condition is true
It always runs every block no matter what

questions.question: An 'If' block has how many main parts?
questions.explanation: An If block has two parts: the condition, and the blocks inside.
options: Two (the condition, and the blocks inside)

questions.question: What are the two parts of an 'If' block?
questions.explanation: The two parts are the condition (the question) and the blocks inside (what to do if yes).
options: The condition (the question) and the blocks inside (what to do if the answer is yes)

questions.question: Which everyday example does the chapter use to explain 'If' statements?
questions.explanation: The chapter uses 'If it's raining, I'll take an umbrella' as its everyday example of an If statement.
options: "If it's raining, I'll take an umbrella."

questions.question: In Cyber Station 3's example, the Turtle moves forward 100 steps and checks a condition. What condition is checked?
questions.explanation: Cyber Station 3 has the Turtle check whether a number is even.
options: Whether the maze has a wall

questions.question: In Cyber Station 3, if the condition (the number is even) is TRUE, what does the Turtle do?
questions.explanation: When the condition is true (the number is even), the Turtle turns right.
options: It turns into a different shape

questions.question: In Cyber Station 3, what does the chapter ask you to figure out about odd numbers?
questions.explanation: Cyber Station 3 explicitly asks 'What happens when the number is odd?' since the If block only runs its action when the condition is true.
options: What happens when the number is odd (since the If block only acts when the condition/even-check is true)
What colour odd numbers should be
How to turn odd numbers into even numbers

questions.question: True or False: An 'If' block only runs its inside blocks when its condition is true.
questions.explanation: This is the exact definition of an If block given in the chapter.

questions.question: Which of these are examples of 'If' statements mentioned in the chapter? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: These three are the chapter's stated If statement examples; deleting the program for a blue Turtle is not mentioned.
options: If there's a coin ahead, collect it
If there's a wall ahead, turn right
If the score is above 100, display "You win!"
If the Turtle is blue, delete the program

questions.question: In the Curiosity Cloud reflection, a video game needs to check something before letting the player advance to the next level. What is checked?
questions.explanation: The Curiosity Cloud reflection is about checking if the player has enough points before advancing.
options: If the player has enough points
If it is raining in the game

questions.question: Why are 'If' statements useful in programs, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: If statements let programs make decisions, making them smarter and more interactive.
options: They let programs make decisions and respond to different situations, making them smarter and more interactive
They make programs run without any instructions
They remove the need for sequences
They always make the program stop

questions.question: In Blockly, where would you find the 'If' block?
questions.explanation: Cyber Station 3 tells students to find the If block in the Logic category.

questions.question: An 'If' statement's condition is best described as:
questions.explanation: A condition is a question, similar to 'Is the score above 5?'.
options: A question, like "Is the score above 5?"

questions.question: True or False: In Blockly, an 'If' block will run its inside blocks even when its condition is false.
questions.explanation: An If block ONLY runs its inside blocks when the condition is true; if the condition is false, those blocks are skipped entirely.

questions.question: The chapter compares an 'If' statement to which kind of everyday thinking?
questions.explanation: The chapter compares If statements to everyday conditional decisions, like the umbrella example.
options: Making decisions based on conditions, like deciding to take an umbrella if it's raining
Following a strict sequence with no choices

questions.question: How many parts does an 'If-Else' block have?
questions.explanation: An If-Else block has three parts.

questions.question: What are the three parts of an If-Else block?
questions.explanation: An If-Else block's three parts are the condition, the If blocks, and the Else blocks.
options: The condition, the 'If' blocks (what to do if yes), and the 'Else' blocks (what to do if no)
The Turtle, the maze, and the finish line
The sequence, the loop, and the variable
The colour, the shape, and the size

questions.question: In an If-Else block, when does the program run the 'Else' blocks?
questions.explanation: The Else blocks run when the condition is false.
options: When the condition is false (the answer is no)

questions.question: Which everyday example does the chapter use for If-Else?
questions.explanation: This is the chapter's stated everyday example of If-Else logic.
options: "If it's raining, take an umbrella, else wear sunglasses."

questions.question: What metaphor does the chapter use to describe how If-Else blocks work?
questions.explanation: The chapter describes If-Else blocks as being like forks in the road.
options: They are like forks in the road, creating multiple paths
They are like a single straight line with no choices
They are like a repeating circle
They are like a locked door

questions.question: In the video game example, if the player does NOT have enough points, what happens according to the If-Else logic?
questions.explanation: If the player doesn't have enough points, the Else path shows 'Try again'.
options: The game deletes the player's progress

questions.question: True or False: An If-Else block only has a condition and blocks for when the condition is true (there is no 'else' option).
questions.explanation: An If-Else block has THREE parts: the condition, the 'If' blocks (for when it's true), AND the 'Else' blocks (for when it's false).

questions.question: Which of these are correct examples of If-Else logic from the chapter? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: These three are the chapter's stated If-Else examples; the Turtle-tired example is not mentioned.
options: If there's a coin ahead, collect it, else keep moving
If raining, take an umbrella, else wear sunglasses
If enough points, go to next level, else show "Try again"
If the Turtle is tired, delete the program, else do nothing

questions.question: According to Milestone B (a True/False check later in the chapter), how many parts does an If-Else block actually have?
questions.explanation: Milestone B corrects a common misconception - stating an if-else has only two parts is FALSE; it actually has THREE parts (condition, if-blocks, else-blocks).

questions.question: True or False: The statement "The if-else block has two parts: condition and what to do if the condition is true" is CORRECT.
questions.explanation: This statement is false, per Milestone B - an if-else block actually has three parts: the condition, the 'if' blocks, and the 'else' blocks.

questions.question: If-Else blocks let a program:
questions.explanation: If-Else blocks let a program handle different situations by creating multiple possible paths.
options: Handle different situations by creating multiple possible paths
Only ever do one single thing
Repeat forever with no stopping condition
